edges.relationship: Gu recalls Liang Qichao’s essays among the readings that shaped his youthful sense of public and scholarly responsibility.
edges.evidence_note: Gu’s own1926preface in Hummel’s1931translation17–18 names two admired Liang essays and places them among other poetry, family, school and political experiences;176 recalls the earlier statecraft ambition. Richter1994,358/n6 separately reports his early journal reading and notes a translation nuance about the wider world. A bounded formative reading, not Liang’s sole influence, later unchanged nationalism, personal teaching or derivation of all source criticism from Liang. Chinese original and Liang essays unread.

edges.relationship: Richter compares Gu and Liang’s late dating of the Laozi against Hu Shi’s earlier chronology.
edges.evidence_note: Named scholarly mediation: Richter1994,373/nn39–42 distinguishes Gu’s style-and-mentality argument, Liang’s late-Warring-States placement and the other distinct participants Qian Mu and Feng Youlan. Hu’s rejection of their evidence is reported and retains Richter’s judgment that he did not establish his own dating. This is an undirected comparison of particular arguments, not a claim that Gu copied Liang or that their complete positions were identical. Original debate texts and Hu’s1933reply (reprinted in1937GushibianVI,387–410) unread.

edges.relationship: Gu limits historical materialism’s use for textual authentication while accepting its value for studying ancient systems and ideology, as Richter reports.
edges.evidence_note: Richter1994,375–376 quotes Gu’s GushibianIIIpreface7–8 and IVpreface22–23. Gu insists on specialist source criticism as a basis for reconstruction and rejects applying historical materialism indiscriminately; he expressly accepts other approaches and its value in appropriate studies. Target is Marxist historiography, not a personal attack on Marx or every Marxist historian. Existing reverse1273reports Li Ji/Liang Yuantong through Dirlik and remains exact. Original Chinese prefaces unread; source-mediated claims retain Richter’s attribution.

edges.relationship: Winter credits Nora’s sites-of-memory project with expanding his evidentiary resources while developing an international, comparative study of mourning.
edges.evidence_note: Own1995book introduction10 explicitly says gained much from extraordinary project and praises brilliant contributions/evidentiary expansion, immediately specifying different objectives.1999 joint37/n54 uses Nora1989 for material memory aids. Particular resource coexists with criticism of national framing and premature obituary of living memory; not influence inferred from similar titles, whole collective assigned to Nora alone or originalNora reading claimed.

edges.relationship: Winter challenges Nora’s national framing and, with Sivan, his claim that living collective memory, ritual and literature have disappeared.
edges.evidence_note: Own1995introduction10 criticizes French-only, antiquarian/reverential framing and lack of systematic comparison while praising project. Joint1999introduction1–3 calls obituary premature, cites living ritual/family narratives/novels and questions generalization beyond France. Joint authorship retained; cited Nora Realms of Memory1996 transArthur Goldhammer distinguished from1989article and collectiveFrench volumes. OriginalNora unread; not blanket denial of sites/material aids or claim all chapters identical.

edges.relationship: Winter and Sivan use Halbwachs’s social framing of individual memory in constructing an account of collective remembrance through group action.
edges.evidence_note: Joint1999p6 explicitly introduces socially framed memory;24–25 explains variable group frameworks and rejects racial/genetic or reified group mind. Positive conceptual resource, qualified by their criticism of strict history/memory split25 and individual/collective blur27. Cited On Collective Memory1992 transLewis A.Coser, The Collective Memory1980 with source-rendered Ditter translation credits (initials uncertain in the rendering), and1997Namer edition retained without claiming original reading. Not sole origin or personal mentorship.

edges.relationship: Winter and Sivan question Halbwachs’s strict division between objective history and subjective memory and the blurred relation between individual and collective remembering.
edges.evidence_note: Joint1999p25 expressly calls distinction impossibly strict and links it to Durkheimian disciplinary hierarchy;27 names problem in Halbwachs’s work while developing agency/Bastide alternative. Halbwachs positive social-framing resource and opposition to reification remain. Critique is joint Winter/Sivan, not every later memory scholar’s view or fresh assessment of entire Halbwachs corpus. n38 references Collective Memorych2 plus Gedi/Elam1996 critique; originals unread.

edges.relationship: Winter and Sivan qualify Durkheimian memory sociology for subordinating history and leaving the individual–collective boundary insufficiently clear.
edges.evidence_note: Joint1999pp23–25 describes social structure alternative to racial/elite-art models but questions history’s subordinate position;27 explicitly says blur is a problem encountered in Durkheim’s and Halbwachs’s work. Bounded qualification within an appreciative reconstruction, not rejection of all sociology or claim Durkheim reduced memory to racial inheritance. Mediation via TerryN.Clark1973 and JohnE.Craig1983, originals unread; coauthor retained.

edges.relationship: Winter uses Benjamin’s angel of history and account of impoverished communicable experience to interpret tradition, catastrophe and traumatic war remembrance.
edges.evidence_note: Own1995 conclusion opening223, freshly checked in2014 publisher reissue extract, explicitly calls thesisIX crucial and image especially apt. Own2000essay in2007reprint385–386 uses Benjamin text on soldiers returning silent to introduce traumatic memory; cited Illuminations1968firstAmerican83–84, checked note gives no editor/translator.1999joint32/35 refers to Benjamin’s anti-consolatory warning through MartinJay’s chapter, not Jay’s original positions silently assigned to Winter. Source calling text1933 remains unverified original chronology. Existinggroup168 preserved; directpersonpair newly proposed, no sole claim to field.

edges.relationship: Fitzpatrick identifies Prost’s treatment of memorials as an important precedent for Winter’s emphasis on consolation before later political appropriation.
edges.evidence_note: Fitzpatrick1997 paragraph The engrossing discussion explicitly says follows admirable example of In the Wake of War1992edition and explains initial/primary vs later appropriation. Named substantive scholarly mediation, originalProst and Winter94–96 unread. Co-resources Mosse/Bushaway/Inglis retained, alongside distinct existingMosse critique. Existing1756undirected shared-method comparison remains; this is particularmemorial-research uptake, not same claim or causality from coauthoring2020book. No guessed translator for1992edition.

edges.relationship: Winter and Sivan credit Burke with a specific Warburg reference and critical comments used in developing their discussion of social memory.
edges.evidence_note: Joint1999p23n28 thanks MarkRussell ANDPeterBurke for drawing attention to Warburg’s ItalianArt/InternationalAstrology reference and critical comments on these points. Specific bounded research contribution, not mere general thanks or claim Burke originated Warburg’s theory; MarkRussell/coauthorSivan retained despite missing endpoints. edges.relationship: Benton explicitly credits Curtin’s world-history training as the foundation for Law and Colonial Cultures and acknowledges his example and continuing mentorship.
edges.evidence_note: Own acknowledgmentsxi recounts Curtin repeatedly urging world rather than narrower Iberian, West African or Atlantic history and states the subsequent training provided the foundation for the later book. This is specific methodological formation, not merely institutional overlap; no claim that Curtin supplied every legal argument or that Benton’s scholarly detours were irrelevant.

edges.relationship: Benton explicitly follows Braudel’s long-century convention to mark continuities that cross ordinary century boundaries in A Search for Sovereignty.
edges.evidence_note: Own4/n5 states this precise adoption and explains varying chronological ranges. Narrow methodological resource only: no assertion of general Annales allegiance, derivation of all legal geography from Braudel, or an independently checked reading of Braudel’s original work.

edges.relationship: Benton names Armitage among the scholars whose work she builds on to complicate conventional accounts of international law, using his analysis of natural and positive law together in the late eighteenth century.
edges.evidence_note: Own6/n10 explicitly credits Armitage alongside Anghie, Keene and Sylvest rather than giving him exclusive credit;6/n11 specifies Declaration of Independence chapter2 as the particular resource.5/n8also quotes his imperium/dominium dilemma;acknowledgmentsxivcredit a Kingsbury/Armitage-convened group with shaping early ideas. Resource is substantive, not based solely on coattendance. Armitage’s books and other named originals unread here.

edges.relationship: Benton draws on Cooper’s account of the uneven distribution of power and economic relations to frame the lumpiness of imperial formations and the possibilities for rewriting global history.
edges.evidence_note: Own8/n14explicitly extends this insight chronologically/methodologically with Cooper’s Globalization essay101;7/n13uses Cooper’s uneven sovereignty discussion as a qualification to territorial narratives. Acknowledgmentsxivcredit Burbank and Cooper jointly for sharing ideas on imperial political imagination, not Cooper alone. Cited original essay/book unread; no claim Cooper originated all of Benton’s spatial argument.

edges.relationship: Benton challenges Agamben’s model of exception by arguing that imperial suspensions of law often substituted or reconfigured legal authorization within layered sovereignty rather than producing an absence of law.
edges.evidence_note: Own Humanity82–83answer explicitly makes this argument through martial law, penal colonies and bare sovereignty. Her account explains how law could sanction violence and does not equate legality with protection. Edelstein’s distinct81claims are not attributed to her. Her final83answer limits direct present-day equivalence and recognizes nineteenth-century changes. Agamben’s originals and Benton’s concluding book chapter remain unread; this is Benton’s specific historical objection, not proof that his entire theory is refuted.

edges.relationship: Benton argues that world-systems accounts centered on economic primacy or Europe–Americas connections can miss the institutional and legal interconnections joining regions, proposing institutional world history as an alternative.
edges.evidence_note: Own2002intro4/n5and6–7/nn9–10 explicitly critiques named variants and Asian-centered inversions as well as Eurocentric approaches. This is scoped criticism of those analytical frameworks, not rejection of every dependency argument or attribution of all cited positions to Wallerstein. Abu-Lughod, Voll and Frank retain their distinct cited roles and are absent person endpoints; no automatic personal Wallerstein arrow.

edges.relationship: Huang Kewu compares Liang’s plural account of historical causation with Weber’s rejection of a single controlling historical factor.
edges.evidence_note: Huang2003 printed196, visually collated, places Liang’s explicit refusal of a sole explanatory principle alongside Weber’s complex, multiple historical causes, contrasting both with Marxist historical materialism. This is Huang’s undirected scholarly comparison. It does not establish Liang read Weber, shared every Weberian position, or derived the conception solely from a European thinker; Huang emphasizes Buddhist and Confucian resources. Note65 cites Liang’s 非唯 in Yinbingshi Wenji41p82; no particular Weber edition is cited in this checked sentence and none is invented. Liang’s original essay and Weber’s works unread; quoted Chinese checked in the mediating paper.

edges.relationship: Maruyama recalls using Marx’s inversion of Hegel as a conceptual analogy for Norinaga’s transformation of Sorai’s thought, then changing the wording after Nanbara warned about its political resonance.
edges.evidence_note: Own August1974retrospective author introductionxviii explicitly identifies the analogy and Marx’s criticism of Hegel in the preface to the second edition of Capital. This is a particular interpretive/metaphorical resource, not a general profession of Marxist identity. Translation of this introduction is Ronald P.Dore, distinct from Hane’s main-book translation. Original Japanese essay, German Marx passage and unrevised manuscript unread; the claim is Maruyama’s later testimony, not independent proof of a1930sreading sequence.

edges.relationship: Maruyama names Weber among the writers who supplied occasional hints for his study of the transition from natural to artificial social order in Tokugawa political thought.
edges.evidence_note: Own author introductionxxix expressly denies any single obvious influence on the PartIIleitmotif while naming Weber alongside Ferdinand Tönnies and Ernst Troeltsch. Scope is exactly these occasional hints, not an exclusive source or derivation of all Maruyama’s rationalization theory. Hane’s separate translator prefaceviiialso reports Maruyama’s position between historicism and empiricism through Weber/Heller/Mannheim, quoting the1963introduction, which remains unread here. Main evidence is own1974retrospective translated by Dore; original Weber works and PartIIchapters unread.

edges.relationship: Maruyama credits Marxist attention to social context and class structure, and Borkenau’s analysis of changing thought categories, as methodological resources for linking the internal development of ideas to social history.
edges.evidence_note: Own author introductionxxiv–xxviandxxvii–xxviiiis explicit about his methodological stimuli and refusal to treat culture/philosophy as self-sufficient. Borkenau is a specifically named resource for nature/reason/law and the norm/nature split, not a synonym for all Marxists or automatic Frankfurt-School affiliation. The group endpoint is Marxist social history; Karl Marx’s particular analogy is separately proposed. Own remarks deny exclusive adherence to any school. Borkenau original and original Japanese texts unread; Dore translation retained.

edges.relationship: Maruyama criticizes Marxist intellectual histories that reduce ideas to class reflections or fail to explain concretely the relation between ideas’ internal logic and changes in the social base, while retaining sympathy for scholars working under repression.
edges.evidence_note: Own author introductionxxiii–xxviiidifferentiates simplistic orthodox-Soviet reductions from more sophisticated Japanese approaches, then objects to unresolved mediation, progressive/reactionary sorting and inferences about popular thought from rebellion records. He also credits scholars’ conscience and anti-authoritarian constraints; this is not rejection of every Marxist method or attribution of all objections directly to Marx. Broad group criticism is distinct from own positive resources and the Karl Marx analogy. Retrospective August1974text translated by Dore; specific criticized originals unread.
